newsitem.title: USA: FBI names chief Adams Library theft suspect.
newsitem.headline: FBI names chief Adams Library theft suspect.

text.p: The FBI used a federal courtroom Monday to name the chief suspect in the theft of four priceless books, including the Mendi bible, from the Adams National Historic Site library.
FBI agent David Nadolski took the witness stand at a probation hearing for Kevin Gildea, 41, and testified that the Quincy, Massachusetts, artist was "the main suspect" in the Nov. 11, 1996, robbery.

Nadolski testified that several days after the break-in at the site, home of Presidents John Adams and his son, John Quincy Adams, a lawyer for Gildea called to say he would aid in the recovery of the four books if the FBI would help him have state burglary charges dropped.
"Your honour," Gildea, who represented himself at the hearing, called out to U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns, "I'm not charged with any of these crimes...
"They're trying to convict me in the press," Gildea said pointing to the rows of reporters in the courtroom.
The FBI called newsrooms earlier Monday alerting them to the hearing saying several FBI agents would testify.

The judge told Assistant U.S. Attorney James Lang, "I agree with Mr. Gildea ... this testimony doesn't have anything to do" with whether he violated the terms of his probation and halted the prosecutor's examination of Nadolski.

But the interruption did not come before Nadolski, a 14-year veteran with the FBI, testified Gildea owned a white 1985 Chevy station wagon with wood sidepanels that is "very close to a description of the car" witnesses near the Adams site gave police.

A U.S. Department of Probation memoradum written by Gildea's probation officer Todd Shelton, who also testified at the hearing, said in part that Gildea "was the chief suspect in the recent burglary at the Quincy Adams historical site in Quincy."
The probation hearing is set to continue on Friday.

The FBI recovered two of the stolen books Jan. 10 -- the 1839 Mendi Bible, given to John Quincy Adams, the nation's sixth president, by 53 Mendi tribesmen he helped free after they mutunied while being transported on a slave ship from West Africa to Cuba, and a Latin version of the King James Bible printed in 1621.
The books were found in a locker at a Portsmouth, New Hampshire, gym.
Still missing were Block's Ichthyology, a natural history book on fish, written in 1785, and a 1882 Bible that belonged to John Quincy Adams' wife, Louisa Catherine.
